wine.name: Dry Riesling
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, blended from the house's own vineyards on Seneca Lake and Keuka Lake, with a little bought fruit in some years.
wine.sites: The estate's slopes above the west shore of Keuka Lake, planted from 1958 on shale and slate, and its vineyard on the shore of Seneca Lake, a few degrees warmer, which gives riper fruit.
wine.making: Pressed and fermented cool in temperature controlled stainless steel tanks with selected yeasts, kept from malolactic conversion so that the acidity stays sharp, and never put in oak. By the house's sheets the wine then rests on its lees for some months before it is bottled.
wine.glass: Lime zest, green apple and grapefruit over wet slate, with a hint of petrol that grows with age; light in body and dry to the taste, with high, mouthwatering acidity and a clean, stony finish.
wine.ageing: Bright and ready on release, it keeps well and gains notes of petrol and honey over five to ten years in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, with lake trout, sushi or a light chicken dish.

records.table: Dr. Konstantin Frank's Dry Riesling comes from the house that showed European vines could live through Finger Lakes winters: estate Riesling from Keuka and Seneca Lakes, fermented cool in steel and never oaked. Expect lime, green apple and wet slate on sharp acidity.
records.story: Konstantin Frank (1899 to 1985), a viticulturist from Odessa who had grown Riesling in the hard winters of Ukraine, reached New York in 1951 with a doctorate in viticulture and, by the house's account, little English. He worked at the Geneva Experiment Station, where he argued against the received view that European vines could not live through the region's cold. In 1953 he met the president of Gold Seal, a French champagne maker who shared his French, and from 1954 the two made experimental plantings that showed grafted vinifera on the right rootstock could come through the winter. In 1958 Frank bought land on the west side of Keuka Lake and planted Riesling and other European varieties, and in 1962 he founded Vinifera Wine Cellars, a name that declared its purpose. His son, who had bought a separate property in 1980 for traditional method sparkling wine, ran the house after his death in 1985, and the family has kept it since, across four generations by its own account. The Dry Riesling carries the founder's argument in a bottle: a vinifera wine of the Finger Lakes that needs no hybrid grape and no excuse, and for a sommelier it is where the region's Riesling story begins.

wine.name: HJW Vineyard Riesling
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, from the estate's own vines in the HJW Vineyard.
wine.sites: The HJW Vineyard, the founder's home site above the west shore of Seneca Lake near Dundee, planted from 1976 to 1978 on shallow topsoil over shale bedrock that keeps yields low; farmed biodynamically, with Demeter certification from 2023.
wine.making: Picked and sorted by hand, pressed as whole clusters and fermented slowly with the vineyard's own yeasts in stainless steel, where it stays for some months before bottling. It is made dry or close to it, with less than a per cent of sugar left in the vintages read.
wine.glass: Lime zest, tangerine peel and green apple over wet shale and white pepper, with a hint of white blossom; taut and lean in body, with high, piercing acidity and a long, stony finish.
wine.ageing: Tight in its first years, it opens after three to five and gains depth for a decade and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly if it seems closed; a white wine glass, with trout, scallops or roast pork.

records.table: Hermann J. Wiemer's HJW Vineyard Riesling comes from the founder's own shale site above Seneca Lake, planted in the late 1970s: hand picked, fermented with its own yeasts in steel and dry or nearly so. Lime, tangerine peel and stone on taut acidity; pour it cool.
records.story: The founder came from Bernkastel on the Mosel, from a family that had made wine there for generations, and trained at Geisenheim. In 1968 he chose the Finger Lakes over the family business and went to work as winemaker at Bully Hill, near Hammondsport on Keuka Lake, where he also began grafting vinifera vines. In 1973 he bought a former soybean farm above the west shore of Seneca Lake near Dundee, where no commercial Riesling then grew, and from 1976 to 1978 he planted Riesling and Chardonnay there, the block that became the HJW Vineyard. His first wines, a Riesling and a Chardonnay of the 1979 vintage, mark the founding of the estate. Beside the cellar he built a grafting nursery that supplied vines to growers across the East. In 2007 he retired and handed the estate to his winemaker, with a Swedish agronomist as partner, and the single vineyard bottlings grew under them. In 2023 the HJW Vineyard gained Demeter certification for biodynamic farming. For a sommelier the HJW Vineyard Riesling shows what one Finger Lakes site on shale gives Riesling: the Mosel's lessons, written in another country's stone.

records.table: Ravines' Argetsinger Vineyard Dry Riesling comes from a steep, old vineyard on limestone above the southeast shore of Seneca Lake, fermented cool in steel and kept on its lees. Key lime, grapefruit and wet stone, dry and taut; pour it with shellfish.
records.story: Ravines was founded by a couple, a European trained winemaker and a chef, who set out to make truly dry Riesling in a region where few made one. The winemaker had been chief winemaker at Dr. Konstantin Frank from 1998. The house's first land was a parcel on the eastern slopes of Keuka Lake between two ravines, which carry cold air and water away from the vines and gave the house its name. Accounts of the founding differ, the land bought in 2000 and the house founded in 2001 or 2002, but by its own account the first vintage, of 2002, was all dry vinifera wine, and its Dry Riesling took the dry Riesling prize at the World Riesling Cup in 2003. From the start, working in a rented barn on Keuka Lake, the house made wine from two sites it had chosen: the Argetsinger Vineyard on Seneca Lake, owned by the Argetsinger family and managed by Ravines, and the 16 Falls Vineyard. In 2010 production moved to a former winery at Geneva, at the north end of Seneca Lake, which the house later bought and renamed Limestone Springs. The Argetsinger wine is the house's argument in one bottle: one Seneca site on limestone, made dry, and for a sommelier a measure of how far Finger Lakes Riesling has travelled from sweetness.

records.table: Boundary Breaks' No. 239 Dry Riesling is a single clone wine: Geisenheim clone 239 from the estate's vineyard at Lodi on Seneca Lake's east shore, chosen for its sharper acidity. Lime, green apple and flint, dry and bright: a lesson in what a clone gives.
records.story: The land on Porter Covert Road at Lodi, on the east side of Seneca Lake, was bought by the Covert family in 1861 and farmed by them for generations. In 2008 the family sold most of the farm to the estate's founder, who found no vines on it and only a half built cabin. The heavy soil, compacted by decades of farming, was deep ripped before planting, and from 2009 the vineyard was planted almost wholly to Riesling, with vines raised by a nursery in California. Rather than one clone, the estate planted several, among them Geisenheim clones 110, 198 and 239, to see how each would show on the site, and it chose to bottle them apart: 239, slightly sharper in acidity, for a dry wine, and 198 for a reserve. By the house's history the young vines were picked for a harvest in 2011. The estate is young and its story short, but it has a clear idea, the clone on the label as other houses print a vineyard, and the No. 239 Dry Riesling carries it. For a sommelier it is a lesson in one glass: a clone, and not only a site, can mark a Riesling, and the Finger Lakes can show both.

wine.name: Classique Dry Riesling
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, blended from growers' vineyards along the east shore of Seneca Lake.
wine.sites: Ten to sixteen lieux dits, by vintage, along an eight mile stretch of the east shore of Seneca Lake, among them sites the house also bottles alone, such as Caywood, Railroad and Willow.

wine.ageing: Ready on release, it gains texture over three to six years and keeps longer in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, with shellfish, roast pork or a light curry.

records.table: Forge Cellars' Dry Riesling Classique blends many vineyards along Seneca Lake's east shore, each fermented with its own yeasts in old barrels, as a Rhône grower would. Bone dry, with plum, lemon oil and wet stone; serve it cool with shellfish.
records.story: Forge Cellars began in 2011 as a partnership between a grower and winemaker of the southern Rhône, of the family that holds Château de Saint Cosme in Gigondas, and American partners, one of whom found the fruit and oversaw the growing. The aim, by the house's account, was bone dry Riesling from Seneca Lake to stand beside the dry Rieslings of Alsace and Germany. The first vintage, of 2011, was a small lot of dry Riesling, and over the following years the house grew to many bottlings, Riesling and Pinot Noir above all, from growers' sites along the east shore. With the 2014 vintage the blend of those sites took the name Classique, while the sites that stood out were bottled alone under their own names. The winery sits high above Burdett on the southeast shore. The method is the Rhône partner's: each site pressed and fermented apart with its own yeasts in neutral barrels, then blended. Forge Cellars is a house of its own, not a branch of Saint Cosme. For a sommelier the Classique shows Seneca Lake's east shore in one glass, read through a European cellar, and it is the house's wine to know before its single sites.
